*Pinguin*German{}|Etymology}Early 17th century. Borrowed,perhaps through from Dutch pinguïn (1595),from English penguin,which originally referred to the now extinct great auk. Further origin uncertain. Probably either from Welsh litwhite head,the great auk having two characteristic white patches near the eyes; or from Latin tfat,plump,referring to the plumpish appearance of both birds. *Plage*German{}|Etymology}From early from Middle High German plāge,from Latin blow,wound. The word was originally chiefly Central German,therefore sometimes secondarily adapted to the Upper German consonantism as (later) from Middle High German pflāge,which form did not last,however. *Priester*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German p1-Ĭ,from Old High German p1-Ĭ,borrowed around 700 (after the High German consonant shift,but before the diphthongisation of West Germanic ''ē'') from pre-from Old French prestre,from Latin presbyter,from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος. from German Presbyter. Immediately cognate with from Dutch p1-Ĭ,from Low German Preester,from French prêtre. Compare also from English priest. *Pustekuchen*German{}|Etymology}Early 20th century,originally Berlin slang. pusten+t1to blow+Kuchen+t2cake,pie. The word  on its own is already attested with the same sense in thieves' cant (Rotwelsch) since 1818,and likely goes back to twise or cunning man,used here with a sense along the lines of “you wise guy!” or “you trickster!”. The first component may be tsimply,but this appears less conclusive. It may also be merely the verb pusten in the sense “to exhale/snort dismissively”; compare the expression jemandem etwas pusten/husten.|Pronunciation}/ˈpuːstəˌkuːxən/}Ⓓc/cb/De-@^.ogg|Interjection}!}#colloquial no way!,not gonna happen!,forget about it!}•Du könntest mich doch abholen… — Ja,'''@^'''! *R*German{}|Pronunciation}letter name/ɛr/+ʔɛʁ+ʔɛɐ̯}phoneme/r/+ʁ+ɾ+ɐ̯+ː}De-&_.OGG|Letter}#The eighteenth letter of the German alphabet.|Usage notes}The letter &_ has a variety of possible realisations in contemporary German. Three positions must be distinguished:}Before vowels,the variation is mostly between a uvular consonant (fricative,approximant,or rarely trill) and an alveolar consonant (trill,flap,or rarely approximant). In northern,central,and south-western Germany,the alveolar pronunciation is now rare and chiefly restricted to the elderly generation of some areas. In south-eastern Germany,Austria,Switzerland,and South Tyrol,it remains more common; but even in these regions the uvular &_ is gaining ground and is already strongly predominant in some parts (e.g. Vienna).}Word-finally and before consonants,most accents may vowelise &_ to IPAchar:ɐ̯~IPAchar:ə̯,but in different ways. Vowelisation is commonest after long vowels and IPAchar:/ə/,where it is also prescribed in the broadcasting standard. A majority of speakers,however,vowelise &_ after short vowels,too. The resulting diphthongs may be contracted and length distinctions before vowelised &_ may be lost. The degree to which this happens differs regionally and idiolectally.}Before the syllable -en IPAchar:/ən/,many speakers also vowelise &_,though this is commonest in fast or casual speech,and consonantal realisations may be retained depending on the rhythm of the phrase as well as the formality of the context.

*Radikalinski*German{}|Etymology}Late 19th century,from radikal+-inski. The latter suffix was also used in some other formations (like Brutalinski),but  is the commonest and perhaps original form. Derived from Slavic surnames,especially from Polish -iński,from Polish -yński (as in from Polish Kaczyński,from Polish Kamiński,from Polish Zieliński,etc.). At the time there could have been an association with Polish nationalist revolutionaries,who were considered enemies of state in the German Empire. However,Slavic surnames have been fairly common in Germany (especially in eastern regions and the Ruhrgebiet),so there need not necessarily have been a particular ethnic or political association.|Pronunciation}/ʁadikaˈlɪnski/|Noun}(mask.,plural:[@^(s)])}#informal a political radical,especially a fugleman or firebrand

*Raffzahn*German{}|Etymology}raffen,(to grab) grasp,snatch up,Zahn,(tooth). The word,in its first sense,is an inherited word whose oldest attested form so far is Late from Middle High German reffzan “incisor” that originally might have applied the probable sense “carnassial,fang,(English); tusk”. The extension to human teeth developed probably by comparison for instance with a from English tusk. From 1800 onwards the word then also applied the second and third sense which semantically overlapped with the sense “snatch up” of the German verb raffen.|Pronunciation}ˈʁafˌt͡saːn}Raff+zahn}Ⓓb/b3/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^es,plural:[Räffzähne])}#colloquial crooked upper incisor jut out,jutting out,(English) under the upper lip}#}'''1936''',Thomas Mann:''Joſeph in Ägypten.'' *rauchen*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German rouchen,from Middle High German röuchen,from Old High German rouhhen,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆raukijan. -en.}The form without umlaut is due to (chiefly Upper German) umlaut hindrance before velars and/or readaptation to the noun. Some dialects use either form throughout,others came to distinguish both forms (transitive vs. intransitive). In the latter case,the umlauted form usually took on the transitive use. In Modern Standard German,räuchen was displaced by the extended form räuchern (see there). The use for “to inhale tobacco” (later 17th c.) is a from French nocap1.|Pronunciation}/ˈʁaʊ̯xən/}Ⓓa/a0/De-@^.ogg|Verb}#intransitive to smoke,give off smoke}•Das abgebrannte Haus '''raucht''' noch immer.}•The burned-down house is still '''smoking'''.}#intransitive to smoke (tobacco etc.)}•Ich '''rauche''' nicht.}•I don’t '''smoke'''.}•Er '''raucht''' eine Zigarette.}•He’s '''smoking''' a cigarette.

*Reuss*German{}|Etymology}From an earlier form Rusa,first attested in 1296.}Ptolemy recorded the river's Pre-Germanic name as from English Silana,which is reflected in the name Silenen. The Germanic name for the river is attested as from English Rusa or from English Rusia from the 9th century,and was occasionally recorded as from English Ursa in the Early Modern period (compare from English Urseren). This name likely derives from the early from German - from Proto-Germanic ⋆Rūsi or the oblique form from Proto-Germanic ⋆Rūsjō-.}Greule (1982) interprets the name as an Old European hydronym,closely related to Riß. Given Ptolemy’s record of the pre-Germanic name Silana,it is possible that only part of the river was known as from English Rūsi in antiquity. Alternatively,from English Rūsi may have been introduced as a Germanic name during the early medieval period,potentially derived from Old High German rūsa,from Old High German tfish trap (see the modern Reuse).}More at @^.|Pronunciation}/ʁɔɪ̯s/}Ⓓ3/36/De-@^.ogg}@^|Proper noun}(fem.)}#@^

*Reuter*German{}|Pronunciation}Ⓓ9/9d/De-@^.ogg|Etymology 1}From Dutch trobber; soldier; cavalryman,from Middle Dutch trobber,looter,from Old French routier,from Old French rote,from Old French route,whence also from German Rotte.
